results.title: OpenAI introduces new image classifier, warning screens to tackle CSAM on ChatGPT
results.content:
Amid mounting scrutiny over the risks posed by AI chatbots to children, OpenAI on Monday, November 16, unveiled new tools to curb child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on ChatGPT, including an AI-powered classifier that can detect CSAM images.

The AI startup also said it is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualises children. It further released new guidelines for developers and a suite of tools for law enforcement agencies as part of its efforts to combat CSAM.

OpenAI does not allow ChatGPT to generate CSAM content and blocks user requests related to it, as per its existing rules. It also permanently bans any ChatGPT user account that repeatedly violates these rules.

The company’s latest move comes at a time when it is facing several lawsuits that blame its AI tools for harming users, especially children. Last month, attorneys general of eight US states sued OpenAI alleging that ChatGPT coached users, including teenagers, to harm themselves or others.

They further claimed that ChatGPT is designed to be agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users. This, in turn, reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behavior and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings, the lawsuits alleged.

Over the past year, OpenAI has announced several changes to its AI chatbot platform. It has published a safety blueprint, updated content guidelines to ban inappropriate AI-generated content, and re-calibrated its AI models to prevent them generating harmful content. Its most notable action came in August 2026, when it launched a specific version of ChatGPT for teen users aged 13–17, with stronger safety protections and features focused on learning.

results.title: OpenAI sued by California over rogue AI hacking attack
results.content:
California is suing OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, following a series of cyber attacks carried out by its AI models during testing.

Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, accused the tech giant of releasing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight in a lawsuit filed in San Francisco’s state court.

OpenAI revealed in July that a rogue bot had broken out of its IT system to attack the technology company Hugging Face.

Mr Bonta said in a statement: “The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability – and this was only one of 80 known incidents.

“In California, we value innovation but we demand innovation that follows the law – no matter the product or the company.”

It is the first state-level legal action over the cyber attacks.

After the breach, OpenAI called the breakout “an unprecedented cyber incident involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities”.

The company acknowledged the need for greater transparency around rogue AI behaviour and promised to reinforce its safeguards.

OpenAI introduced a new incident disclosure framework on Sept 16, committing to transparency “even when significance is uncertain”.

The company and its competitors have reported several other AI agent breakouts – frequently weeks or months after the fact – and occasionally only after independent researchers brought them to light.

These breaches have intensified pressure on Donald Trump’s administration and US legislators to mitigate AI threats, particularly to emergency services and the energy and banking sectors.

Congress is considering federal regulations, including proposed legislation that would mandate independent security audits for the most advanced AI models.

Separately, OpenAI is fighting numerous lawsuits concerning user safety.

A bipartisan group of eight states sued the developer last month, claiming ChatGPT encouraged users including teenagers to harm themselves or others.

results.title: California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards
results.content:
California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards.

The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet.

It proceeded to launch a days-long cyberattack on the AI hosting platform Hugging Face.

In the California complaint, Bonta argues that the incident indicates that OpenAI pursues growth over guardrails, leading to potentially dangerous errors.

“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit is the first brought by a state in response to the July incident. It alleges that OpenAI violated California’s consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance through its actions.

The complaint, filed in a state court in San Francisco, calls for civil penalties against OpenAI and an injunction to bar it from engaging in actions that constitute “unfair competition”.

“The simple truth is that the attack was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s decision to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” the complaint reads.

The Hugging Face incident became a catalyst for anxieties in the US about the explosive growth of the AI industry and the relatively light oversight it receives from the government.

President Donald Trump’s administration has largely opposed blanket regulations on the AI industry, warning that such rules could stifle the industry’s growth.

In December 2025, for instance, Trump issued an executive order attempting to limit the ability of individual states to pass laws that might govern AI development.

results.title: SpaceX Just Brought a Starship Back From Orbit and Caught It. Here's the Part of the Business That Gains the Most.
results.content:
## How soon could costs drop?

Probably not right away.

"I think we'll need a few hundred V3 satellites for people to really feel the impact," SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said on the company's third-quarter earnings call in October. She thinks SpaceX can get there by the middle of next year.

Starship has delivered 52 V3 satellites on its two orbital flights, 26 apiece, so every 100 more takes about four flights. If each flight used up a new ship, every load of satellites would carry the cost of a whole upper stage. A ship that's caught and flown again spreads that cost over many launches.

Friday's close puts SpaceX at around $1.9 trillion. Using annualized third-quarter revenue, the stock trades at around 32 times sales. At that valuation, I think investors are already paying for a large share of the savings a reusable Starship could deliver.

Saturday's catch got SpaceX closer to those savings. But they won't show in Starlink's depreciation until caught ships fly again, and the booster still needs to come home on the same flight as the ship. I'd want to see both before paying this much for the shares.

results.title: What Elon Musk's SpaceX Starship Catch Means for Moon Missions
results.content:
## What Happens Next?

SpaceX is expected to inspect the recovered spacecraft and continue testing the upgraded Starship system, while also investigating the loss of the Super Heavy booster. The company must demonstrate reliable recovery of both stages, repeatable orbital missions, docking and large-scale propellant transfer.

NASA and SpaceX are also working toward an uncrewed lunar demonstration of Starship HLS before astronauts use the vehicle. NASA says its HLS program is working toward returning astronauts to the Moon by 2028, although NASA’s Office of Inspector General has continued to raise concerns about the technical challenges and schedule risks facing the HLS program.

Saturday’s catch shows that a spacecraft the size of Starship *can* return from orbit and be recovered directly at its launch site which is a remarkable leap towards reusable spaceflight.

But America’s return to the Moon will depend on whether SpaceX can turn one spectacular recovery into a dependable chain of launches, dockings and fuel transfers in orbit.

results.title: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
results.content:
Nearly a decade ago, Elon Musk gave Tesla’s design team an unusual assignment: Build a sports car that can fly.

Mr. Musk brought in a small team of engineers from SpaceX, his rocket company, to lend a hand. Led by Bill Riley, SpaceX’s executive overseeing engineering on the rocket intended to land NASA astronauts on the moon, the team juggled their day jobs with outfitting a Roadster sports car with cold-gas thrusters, a technology more commonly found in rockets that has enough force to burst a human eardrum, according to three people familiar with the project.

This year, as engineers from both companies prepared for the car’s debut, they spent months putting it through its paces at SpaceX’s rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, the people said. In October, a driverless Roadster did a kick flip in midair, launching off a ramp more than 60 feet high.

This is “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company” Mr. Musk told the crowd.

The flying car demonstration offered a rare glimpse into how the world’s richest person has already created unusual cooperations between his two companies — which he now hopes to merge into a conglomerate valued at more than $3 trillion.

For years, Mr. Musk has quietly shuffled executives and engineers between Tesla and SpaceX to work on his passion projects, blurring the lines between the two, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential business matters. The arrangements highlight how Mr. Musk treated the huge companies as interchangeable parts of a single empire, long before shareholders have been asked to vote on combining them.

results.title: Nvidia shares set for $335 billion swing after earnings, options show
results.content:
By Laura Matthews

NEW YORK, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Options traders are pricing in a roughly $335 billion swing in Nvidia's market value after the company reports third-quarter earnings on Tuesday afternoon, the latest sign of the uncertainty clouding the giant chip firm's outlook.

Nvidia shares have tumbled since CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week following reports he had affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and with a subordinate at Nvidia. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent successor.

The selloff has reduced the chip maker's market value to about $3.9 trillion on Friday from about $5.8 trillion in early October, according to LSEG data. Shares were down 4% on Monday.

Options traders were pricing in a 8.5% move in either direction on Wednesday, a day after the company reports results, more than twice the stock's average post-earnings move over the past eight quarters and just shy of the 8.74% gain following its previous report, according to Susquehanna.

The implied move exceeds the individual market value of about 90% of S&P 500 constituents.

Investors have been trimming Nvidia stock holdings ahead of earnings while continuing to buy call options and call spreads to participate in a potential rebound, said Chris Murphy, co-head of derivatives strategy at Susquehanna. A call option gives holders the right, but not the obligation, to buy the stock at certain price before the contract expires; a call spread involves buying a call option and selling another call option at a different price but with the same expiration.

Advertisement

"Earnings are the main catalyst over the next three days, but that pricing also captures ongoing headline risk — including new company developments and Trump comments — rather than earnings alone," Murphy said.

US President Donald Trump said he would not oppose Huang's return as Nvidia CEO, while a petition calling for his return gathered more than 178,000 signatures, including from prominent Silicon Valley executives. Nvidia's board is not weighing a return for Jensen Huang as CEO, three people told Reuters.

Nvidia also announced on Tuesday that it is forming a committee to oversee the company's national security policies amid allegations that its former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a woman suspected of being an intelligence asset for China.

Nvidia's Board of Directors said it is establishing the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a day after the U.S. Departments of Justice and Commerce gave an update about their joint investigation into Megaspeed, a tech company that once employed the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, Alice Huang.

In a joint statement, the DOJ and the Department of Commerce said that Megaspeed will be brought to the "fullest extent of the law" for "any criminal conduct that may have occurred."

Nvidia's board said its new standing committee will be "responsible for board-level oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management."

The board noted that the company's existing National Security Team and its Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the new interim CEO, Colette Kress, "on day-to-day operations."

The committee will be chaired by Suzanne Nora Johnson, an Nvidia board member and a retired vice chairman of The Goldman Sachs Group.

"NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the DOJ and the Department of Commerce said its investigation of alleged export control violations by Megaspeed began in 2024. The Singaporean cloud-computing company has come under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.

The Commerce Department, according to the joint statement released on Monday, requested records from Nvidia in May 2025 concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Megaspeed was then placed on Nvidia's "no sell" list in June 2025, according to the departments.

# Jensen Huang breaks silence, says he would return as Nvidia CEO

Less than a week after resigning from Nvidia and with a looming appearance in front of Congress, former CEO Jensen Huang finally broke his silence, saying he would be willing to return to the tech giant if asked to do so.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement posted on X. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang’s comments on Tuesday, Nov. 17, are the first since he resigned from Nvidia amid allegations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, replaced him and is serving as the company's interim CEO while the board of directors searches for Jensen Huang's permanent successor.

# Jensen Huang says he’d return as Nvidia CEO if board allows it

Former Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, who was ousted from the world’s largest chipmaker last week, said he’s received an outpouring of support and is willing to run the company again if the board would allow it.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” he said in a statement Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

The company cut ties with Huang after the revelation that he’d had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who the US government reportedly believed was spying on behalf of China.

“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang said in Tuesday’s statement. “I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.”

Since his exit, President Donald Trump and influential executives have called for his return. In a social media post, investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time” and the uncertainty created by his departure in urging the board to take a “slow, measured, and deliberate” approach to Nvidia’s future leadership.

That should include “the potential return of Jensen Huang,” Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker wrote in a letter to Nvidia’s board posted on X. SpaceX and Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk has also expressed support for a comeback.

OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further, but it’s proceeding carefully, according to a summary of deliberations of its recent decision to raise its key policy rate for the first time since 2023.

According to the report, the council acknowledged it faced considerable uncertainty and said it would take its monetary policy decisions one meeting at a time.

The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation.

The summary says the council members agreed that monetary policy cannot lower global energy prices, but can prevent them from leading to generalized inflation.

The decision came as the Bank of Canada raised its outlook for the annual inflation rate to hit 3.5 per cent at the end of this year and remain above three per cent for much of 2027.

The summary of deliberations said higher costs largely haven’t been passed through to consumers so far, but the bank’s surveys suggest businesses expect to raise some prices over the next year.

• "With the Bank’s preferred inflation measures still very well behaved, this is unlikely to be a repeat of the 2022 tightening cycle," Shaun Cathcart, CREA’s senior economist, said in a statement. "Rather, it is more likely to be of the mild to moderate variety, although that distinction does carry extra weight in times of stretched affordability.”

results.title: Could California electric vehicle owners face a new federal fee?
results.content:
## Californians led the nation in electric vehicle adoption

The new fees would hit Californians the hardest as the Golden State leads the nation in electric vehicle adoption.

"California had the largest share of households—about 14%, that owned or leased electric vehicles (EVs), more than twice as many as the national estimate (5.5%)," according to results from the U.S. Census Bureau's 2025 American Community Survey (ACS) 1-year estimates released last month.

Across the nation, about 7.3 million households reported that at least one of their vehicles was an all-electric or plug-in hybrid electric vehicle.

Despite a lapse in federal incentives, the California Energy Commission announced in January that Californians purchased more than 2.5 million cumulative new zero-emission vehicles in 2025.

Tricia Holley, a survey statistician at the Census Bureau said in a statement that California had the highest rate of EV adoption per household, followed by Washington, Hawaii and Nevada.

"And when we look at the county level, Santa Clara County in California led the nation with about 24% of households reporting having an EV," Holley added.

The zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) market in California is buoyed with a diversity of options, with the commission noting that 149 ZEV models were available in California during the last quarter of 2025.

California also has over 200,000 public and shared private EV charging across the state.

results.title: Motorway service stations build solar farms to cope with electric cars
results.content:
The Moto boss recently returned from a five-day fact-finding tour of Shanghai and came back dazzled by high-tech features, such as robotic battery-swapping setups, plus rock-bottom vehicle and charging prices.

“I’ve just been over to Shanghai ... looking at what they have been doing with regard to EV, the quality of the cars, the investment they’ve made in technology, the investment they’ve made in the customer experience, and the price point,” he said. “I mean, they are just fantastic.”

Mr McMeikan was equally forthright about Whitehall’s domestic fiscal policy, warning that EV drivers – especially those without driveways – are being penalised by government tariffs on public chargers.

While motorists with driveways pay zero VAT (temporarily reduced from 5pc) to recharge at home, those relying on public chargers pay the full 20pc rate.

Topping up a typical, midrange 70-kilowatt-hour EV from 20pc to 80pc capacity costs as little as £7 at home with an EV tariff.

But on a fast public charger, that same top-up costs around £45, with much of that cost driven by VAT and surging standing charges that service stations must pay under rules imposed by regulator Ofgem.

For a rapid charging hub with six chargers and 12 connections, standing charges are rising from £19,000 in 2021 to £170,000 in 2027, according to Fast Charge, an industry newsletter.

Mr McMeikan has been lobbying for ministers to cut VAT and other fees on EVs charging beyond the home.

“We’ve been campaigning and we’ve had no cut-through… every time we’ve raised it, it’s just been stonewalled.”

Transport officials and ministers at the energy department tried to tell Mr McMeikan to focus instead on installing more chargers. Still, Mr McMeikan was adamant that the VAT double standard makes no sense.

“If what the Government and the various departments were trying to do was encourage and support the transition to clean energies and electric vehicles, then that would have been another sensible incentive ... Why should you have to pay 15pc more on electricity just because it’s coming from a charger away from home?”

results.title: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility wins Earthshot Prize 2026 for promoting electric vehicles in India
results.content:
Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], November 17 (ANI): India’s efforts to promote electric vehicles have received global recognition, with Mahindra Last Mile Mobility Limited (MLMML) winning the Earthshot Prize 2026 in the ‘Clean Our Air’ category. The company was among five winners announced at the sixth edition of the awards ceremony held in Mumbai.

The award, founded by Britain’s Prince William, comes with a grant of £1 million (approximately Rs 11 crore) for each winner to help expand their work.

Announcing Mahindra’s win, The Earthshot Prize shared a post on X, stating that the company had put more than 4,00,000 electric vehicles on Indian roads by focusing on electric transport for short-distance travel. The post read, “Mahindra Last Mile Mobility (@MahindraLMM) is the Winner of The Earthshot Prize 2026 to Clean our Air.By electrifying India’s “last mile”, they’ve put more than 400,000 electric vehicles on the road. The £1 million prize will help them expand across Asia and Africa.”

Apart from Mahindra, four other winners were announced across different categories.

Niue Ocean Wide Trust won the ‘Revive Our Oceans’ category for its work in ocean conservation. The organisation sells Ocean Conservation Commitments, with each commitment helping protect one square kilometre of ocean for 20 years. The prize money will support its plan to build a NZ$32 million endowment.

In the ‘Build a Waste-Free World’ category, PFAS-Free France was named the winner. The group led a campaign that resulted in France introducing the world’s first national law banning PFAS, also known as ‘forever chemicals’. The £1 million grant will help encourage other countries to take similar steps.

Ørsted won the ‘Fix Our Climate’ category. The company, which is the world’s largest offshore wind operator, has reduced its own emissions by more than 98%. The prize money will support its continued work towards clean energy.

results.title: My Condo Wants Charging Spots for Electric Cars. How Do We Add Them Fairly?
results.content:
**Q: I live in Washington, D.C., in a 150-unit condominium with approximately 150 parking spaces spread over three below-grade levels. We have one or two spaces for our full-time staff, which are necessary, given our busy neighborhood. There’s increasing demand for charging spaces for electric vehicles in our building, and we would like to accommodate them, but how do we do this? Are there apps that can manage the spaces, making sure these spaces are used efficiently?**

**A:** Installing EV charging in your building can be a group project, and you’ll likely need buy-in from your association and building management.

“There’s a lot of nuance and complexity here,” said Ron Kaltenbaugh, president of the Electrical Vehicle Association of Greater Washington, DC, a volunteer organization.

You’ll need an idea of which spaces to use. This can be difficult if all of the parking spaces are owned, and there are none available for shared charging. In some cases, it’s possible for owners to pay to install chargers in their own spots.

You also must review what your bylaws say about parking and EV charging.

When you establish which spaces you will use — if they will be shared among EV owners or if owners will electrify their own spaces — you should hire an electrician or EV charging consultant who can check your existing electrical capacity and determine the best path forward. The consultant can help determine the level of vehicle charging that is the best fit for your building.

In a 150-unit condominium, the practical path, from an efficiency and financial perspective, is to pursue shared Level 2 chargers, rather than putting one charger in every individually owned parking space, said Robert Borkowski, owner of Plug IO, which installs EV chargers in multifamily housing. Coordinating with the electrical utility is usually required.

results.title: Prince William Brings Climate Prize to India, in an Electric Rickshaw
results.content:
It was a royal chariot for the moment.

But when Prince William pulled up to the promenade in the Indian coastal city of Mumbai behind the wheels of a three-wheeled electric rickshaw, with Catherine, Princess of Wales, as his passenger, it was another point he was making. His argument was that the solutions to some of the most pressing environmental challenges, such as clean air, could come from scaling up technology that already exists.

That this year the heir to the British throne has brought his six-year-old Earthshot Prize, which aims to promote creative solutions to the climate crisis, to India seems fitting. This country, with its 1.4 billion people, is a frontier for both the devastating impact of an increasingly erratic climate (more than 80 percent of the region around Mumbai is in drought), and the search for ways to mitigate that impact.

The prize’s five winners were announced at a ceremony hosted by the Indian filmmaker Karan Johar. Each will receive one million pounds, about $1.3 million.

The organizers also hope to offer wider benefits to the winners, in the form of recognition and a connection to business and political leaders.

“The people with the answers are already out there,” Prince William told a gathering of the finalists on Monday. “Our task is to find them, back them and help them scale.”
